plain: The boundary that holds Entra ID, licenses, Teams policies, and verified domains for one organization.
why: An SBC paired in the wrong tenant is a different phone system.
config: Confirm the tenant before you run Connect-MicrosoftTeams.
fault: Two engineers edit two tenants and each thinks the other broke the trunk.

plain: A domain added and proven in the tenant. Direct Routing SBC FQDNs must live on one of these domains.
why: onmicrosoft.com cannot carry the SBC name.
config: Add the domain, including a sip subdomain, before you pair the gateway.
fault: Pairing fails because sbc.contoso.com was never verified.

plain: The default tenant domain. It is not a supported domain for a Direct Routing SBC FQDN.
why: People try it because it already resolves inside Microsoft 365.
config: Use a domain you verified, such as contoso.com.
fault: The gateway object is rejected or never becomes healthy.

plain: Direct Routing users must be homed in Microsoft 365, not left on a Skype for Business on-premises registrar.
why: A user who looks licensed and still is not online will not use the online voice route.
config: Check the user’s registrar before you assign a voice routing policy.
fault: The policy is assigned and the call never leaves the legacy system.

plain: A coexistence mode. Direct Routing is not supported for users in Islands mode.
why: It is a hard stop, not a tuning problem.
config: Move the user to a supported mode before you test PSTN.
fault: PSTN fails only for the Islands users and nowhere else.

plain: The identity directory for the tenant. Teams users, resource accounts, and admin roles are Entra objects.
why: Voice licenses attach to these objects.
config: Create the user or resource account here, then license it, then grant policies.
fault: A resource account exists in Teams and has no license because nobody looked in Entra.

plain: A disabled-for-sign-in Entra account that represents an auto attendant or a call queue. It is not a human login.
why: The published number is often this account, not a person.
config: Create it with a Teams admin role and the User Administrator role.
fault: Agents try to sign in as the queue and the sign-in is correctly blocked.

plain: The Teams voicemail service. It deposits messages in the user’s Exchange mailbox.
why: No mailbox means no voicemail, even when the call routed.
config: Confirm the mailbox and the voicemail policy before you debug the SBC.
fault: Callers hear a greeting failure and the SBC trace is clean.

plain: The license capability that lets a user use Teams as a phone system. It is not, by itself, a PSTN carrier.
why: People say Phone System, Calling Plan, and Teams Premium as if they were one SKU.
config: Assign Teams Phone, then add a connectivity option.
fault: Outbound PSTN fails because only Teams, not Teams Phone, is assigned.

plain: A Microsoft-operated PSTN option. Domestic, international, and pay-as-you-go are the usual flavors. It is an extra license on top of Teams Phone.
why: E5 may include the phone-system capability and still not include a Calling Plan.
config: Buy the plan only where Microsoft sells it, and assign it to the user.
fault: A user in an unsupported country is given a Calling Plan SKU that cannot be used.

plain: The license that provides dial-in numbers for meetings. It is not Teams Phone.
why: Without it, outbound conference calls can route through Direct Routing.
config: Assign it to people who must publish a dial-in number.
fault: Conference dial-out hits the SBC and the carrier bill surprises finance.

plain: An add-on for advanced meetings and related features. It does not replace Teams Phone or a Calling Plan.
why: Interview traps treat it as the PSTN license.
config: Buy it only for the meeting features you actually need.
fault: A design removes Calling Plans because Premium was purchased.

plain: The license each auto attendant or call queue resource account needs, even when the account has no phone number. Subscriptions with Teams Phone include a zero-cost allotment you still have to acquire.
why: Do not put Teams Phone Standard on a resource account.
config: Assign this license. If you swap off Teams Phone Standard, remove and add in the same license change.
fault: Queues die after a two-step license swap.

plain: A Calling Plan billed on use. Also the funding pattern, with communications credits, for some voice-app outbound calls.
why: External transfers from a queue are not free just because users have Direct Routing.
config: Fund the resource account when the attendant or queue sends calls to an external number, uses callback, or places on-behalf calls.
fault: Overflow to a mobile number fails and the user Calling Plan is blamed.

plain: A balance used when a call is not covered by a Calling Plan minute. Voice apps use it for some outbound cases.
why: An empty balance looks like a routing failure.
config: Fund the balance and assign it where the prerequisite article requires it.
fault: The queue worked in the pilot week and stopped when the credit ran out.

plain: A pattern where users place outbound PSTN calls through a resource account’s number instead of each having a number.
why: It is not a free substitute for every Calling Plan scenario. The shared number has its own license rules.
config: Read the current shared-calling prerequisites before you promise it to a site.
fault: Every user was left numberless and the resource account was never funded.

plain: A shared handset. On Direct Routing it does not need a Calling Plan license.
why: People copy a user bundle onto a hallway phone.
config: License the device for Teams and the phone scenario you chose, then assign the number.
fault: A Calling Plan was purchased for every corridor phone on a Direct Routing design.

plain: Rooms use their own SKU family, not a borrowed user Calling Plan. Names such as Basic and Pro change. Check the current name.
why: A room that cannot join is often a license or a resource account, not a codec.
config: Assign the current room license to the room account and keep Conditional Access from blocking the device.
fault: The room account has a user E5 stack and still fails sign-in policy.

plain: Entra policy that can block a phone or a room that is not in the trusted device set.
why: Voice engineers see a SIP 200 and a device that never registers.
config: Exclude or scope device sign-in on purpose. Do not turn Conditional Access off as a test you leave in place.
fault: Rooms fail on Monday after a security change nobody told voice about.

plain: Microsoft’s network guidance prefers a short path to the Microsoft network, without a proxy in the media path.
why: A proxy that was fine for web traffic adds jitter to RTP.
config: Egress Teams media locally. Do not hairpin a branch through a distant data center unless you mean to.
fault: One city’s CQD is poor and the firewall team finds a proxy.

plain: Microsoft recommends that you avoid sending real-time Teams media through a VPN. QoS on the VPN does not fix the extra delay.
why: Split-tunnel designs exist so media can go direct while other traffic stays on the VPN.
config: Test a call on the VPN and off it before you blame the carrier.
fault: Every remote user shows high RTT and the office does not.

plain: Teams does not require ExpressRoute. Local internet egress is the usual design. If you do use ExpressRoute, follow the current network article rather than assuming media is happier there.
why: A contract for ExpressRoute is not a QoS design.
config: Decide the path, then mark DSCP on the path you actually use.
fault: Media was forced onto a long private path and RTT jumped.

plain: The Teams admin center setting that allows clients to insert DSCP. Without it, a correct ACL still sees unmarked client traffic from managed endpoints that honor the policy.
why: Mac and mobile hard-code some marks. Windows follows policy.
config: Turn the insert-markers setting on, then verify at the WAN edge.
fault: The network is marked and the clients were never told to mark.

plain: Microsoft’s planning note: keep the client-to-network-edge path short, on the order of three to five hops, and the ISP-to-Microsoft edge short as well.
why: Each extra hop is a place a mark can be stripped.
config: Draw the path before you buy bandwidth.
fault: A branch hairpins through HQ and then out, adding hops and delay.

plain: G.711 at 20 ms is 160 bytes of payload plus 40 bytes of IP, UDP, and RTP. That is 80 kbit/s per direction.
why: People quote 64 kbit/s and under-size the link.
config: Multiply by concurrent calls and by two directions when both ways are busy.
fault: Thirty calls were planned at 64 kbit/s and the link saturated.

plain: Add an 18-byte Ethernet header to the G.711 20 ms packet and the figure is 87.2 kbit/s per direction.
why: WAN sizing that stops at layer 3 is already short on a LAN you police.
config: Use 87.2 kbit/s when the policer sees Ethernet.
fault: The policer drops the header you forgot.

plain: A certified carrier manages PSTN for you inside the tenant. You need Teams Phone. You do not need a Microsoft Calling Plan or your own SBC.
why: It is the low-operations option when your carrier is in the program.
config: Enable the operator in the admin center and assign the numbers they provide.
fault: Someone also builds a Direct Routing SBC for the same numbers and the routes fight.

plain: The India-specific operator model. It exists because India PSTN rules are not the same as a generic Operator Connect deployment.
why: A global design that ignores it will fail a regulatory review.
config: Use the current India plan article and the licensed operator there.
fault: A UK SBC was proposed as the egress for an India office.

plain: The user’s mobile SIM number is also their Teams number, through a certified mobile operator. Teams Phone is required.
why: It fits frontline and mobile workers, not a reception queue.
config: Assign the operator number to the user. Do not also treat it as a spare Calling Plan.
fault: One human has two different caller IDs and the CRM matches neither.

plain: You connect a certified SBC to Teams and bring your own carrier. Users need Teams and Teams Phone. They must be homed online. Islands mode is not supported.
why: This is the option when you still own trunks, a PBX, analog, or a contact-center SBC.
config: Pair the FQDN, open 5061, allow media ranges, assign a voice route.
fault: The SBC is up and the user has no voice routing policy.

plain: One tenant may use Calling Plans, Operator Connect, Teams Phone Mobile, and Direct Routing at the same time for different users.
why: A global voice policy that assumes one carrier will misroute someone.
config: Give each population a policy that matches its carrier.
fault: A mobile user matches a Direct Routing route and hairpins.

plain: For commercial Microsoft 365, signal to sip.pstnhub.microsoft.com, then sip2, then sip3, on TCP 5061. GCC High and DoD use different names.
why: DNS can return one address. The firewall must allow the published ranges, not that one answer.
config: Allow 52.112.0.0/14 and 52.120.0.0/14 as published on the plan page, and re-check the page when you change firewalls.
fault: A lockdown allows only today’s DNS answer and the trunk fails next week.

plain: UDP 3478–3481 and 49152–53247 between the SBC and the media processors, unless media bypass keeps the media off that path.
why: People open 5061 and forget media, so signaling works and audio does not.
config: Budget at least two media ports per concurrent call on the SBC.
fault: Calls connect and both sides hear silence.

plain: Microsoft does not support changing the media target in the middle of an active Direct Routing call.
why: A clever SBC feature that moves media mid-call will not be a supported troubleshooting step.
config: Negotiate media at setup and leave it.
fault: Audio dies when a transfer tries to move the RTP peer.

plain: Microsoft’s planning tip: allocate at least two media ports on the SBC for each concurrent call.
why: Port exhaustion looks like random one-way audio.
config: Size the SBC media range from the busy-hour call count.
fault: The 51st call connects with no audio.

plain: The dial plan rewrites what a person dialed into a number the routes can match, usually E.164. The first matching rule wins.
why: A route for +44 will never see 020.
config: Put the specific rules above the general ones.
fault: A catch-all rule is first, so the emergency rule never runs.

plain: A set of normalization rules you assign to users. A user can have a more specific plan than the tenant default.
why: Two sites that dial local numbers differently need two plans, not one heroic route.
config: Grant the plan to the user and test from that user.
fault: You edit the global plan and a branch with its own plan does not change.

plain: A name that links a voice routing policy to one or more voice routes. The policy’s ordered list of usages is the permission to place those calls.
why: Usages are how you let one site call internationally and another not.
config: Create the usage, attach routes, then put the usage on the policy in the right order.
fault: International works because the international usage was left on a branch policy.

plain: A number pattern plus an ordered list of SBC gateways. It does nothing until a PSTN usage on the user’s policy points at it.
why: The pattern is a regular expression, not a CUCM route-pattern wildcard.
config: Anchor the pattern. Test with the normalized number, not the raw digits.
fault: The route expects 10 digits and the dial plan already added +1.

plain: The per-user list of PSTN usages, in order. Teams walks that order when it looks for a route.
why: Granting the wrong policy is the most common ‘the SBC is broken’ ticket.
config: Grant it to a test user and read it back with Get-CsOnlineUser.
fault: The pilot user is still on the global policy, which has no usages.

plain: Each voice route lists SBCs with a priority. Lower priority number is tried first in this campus’s teaching model. Confirm the current article before you depend on a tie.
why: Failover is a list, not a wish.
config: Put the local SBC first and a remote SBC second, then pull the cable in a maintenance window.
fault: Both gateways are priority 1 and nobody knows which one took the call.

plain: 999, 112, and 911 must be normalized on purpose. A general rule that runs first can swallow them.
why: An emergency call that matches an international route is a design defect.
config: Put emergency rules above catch-alls, and give them a route that is always present.
fault: A user dials 999 and the dial plan turns it into an extension.

plain: A voice app that answers, plays a greeting, and routes by schedule, menu, directory, or operator.
why: It is the front door. A broken menu is a broken company number.
config: Create the attendant, attach a licensed resource account, then assign a number only if the PSTN must reach it.
fault: The menu option points at a queue that has no agents and no overflow.

plain: A voice app that holds callers and offers them to agents by attendant, serial, round robin, or longest idle routing.
why: Presence can skip someone who is already busy, which changes who ‘should’ have rung.
config: Set timeout and overflow before you publish the number.
fault: The timeout is 3 seconds and callers always overflow.

plain: A queue behavior where the caller stays in the conference while agents are tried, so the transfer is faster and the greeting is not replayed the same way.
why: Turning it off changes the caller experience and the failure sound.
config: Test both modes with a real agent client before you argue about delay.
fault: Callers hear silence while the queue hunts, and someone disables the queue.

plain: Where the call goes when the queue is full or the timeout expires. It can be a person, another voice app, voicemail, or an external number.
why: An external overflow needs funding on the resource account.
config: Name the overflow in the design, then test it by making every agent busy.
fault: Overflow to a mobile fails and the queue itself is blamed.

plain: An attendant feature that lets a caller reach a person by name or extension.
why: It exposes the directory you did not mean to publish.
config: Scope who can be found. Do not leave the default if the tenant has privileged accounts.
fault: A caller reaches an executive because directory search was on.

plain: A calendar the attendant uses to play the closed greeting. It is not the same object as business hours.
why: A holiday that is only in someone’s memory is an open company on that day.
config: Load the next year’s holidays when you build the attendant.
fault: The office is closed and the attendant still hunts the queue.

plain: Teams picks a civic address from the network location it can see: trusted IP, site, and subnet in the usual design.
why: A VPN address must not inherit the headquarters address.
config: Build the topology, assign addresses, and test from a known subnet.
fault: A laptop on the VPN reports the HQ floor.

plain: The street address you validate for emergency calling. A dispatchable location is specific enough for responders.
why: A campus with one address and five buildings is not specific.
config: Validate the address and tie subnets to places inside it.
fault: The PSAP gets a city and no building.

plain: An address that means ‘this client is inside our network.’ It is how Teams decides the client is on a site you mapped.
why: If the trusted IP is the VPN concentrator, every remote user looks internal.
config: List the real internet egress addresses, not the VPN pool, unless you mean to.
fault: Remote users inherit a building.

plain: Controls notification and how the client looks up location. It is not the PSTN route.
why: You can have a perfect policy and still send the call to the wrong SBC.
config: Pair the policy with a routing policy and a tested number from the carrier.
fault: Security is notified for a test call and the route still left the country.

plain: You, the SBC, and the carrier deliver the emergency call. Microsoft does not become the emergency carrier because Teams is the client.
why: PIDF-LO may be present. The carrier still has to accept the call.
config: Build an emergency voice route that prefers the local SBC.
fault: 999 matches an international route via another country.

plain: With Microsoft Calling Plans in supported countries, Microsoft’s emergency calling service is part of the plan. You still configure locations.
why: Direct Routing habits do not apply unchanged.
config: Assign the Calling Plan and the emergency addresses for those users.
fault: A Calling Plan user is sent to your SBC for 911 by a copied route.

plain: Stops a user in a regulated site from placing a PSTN call through a gateway in another site. It is a toll-bypass control.
why: Media bypass can fight it if media would egress in the wrong place.
config: Enable it per site with the network topology and the gateways that belong there.
fault: A traveler’s laptop in one country egresses through another country’s SBC.

plain: A Direct Routing appliance that can keep local PSTN calling when the branch cannot reach Microsoft 365.
why: It is not a full Teams cloud. Meetings and presence are not the survivable feature set.
config: Deploy a supported appliance, point the local clients at it, and test a WAN cut.
fault: The office loses the WAN and nobody can call emergency services.

plain: Media can flow between the Teams client and the SBC, skipping Microsoft’s media processors. Signaling still goes through Teams.
why: People hear ‘bypass’ and think the SBC talks to Teams with no SIP proxy.
config: Enable it on the gateway only when the client can reach the SBC and LBR does not forbid the path.
fault: Bypass is on for a VPN user and audio is worse than the processor path.

plain: A Direct Routing pattern with internal and external SBC interfaces so a branch user stays on the local media path.
why: It is more specific than a single bypass flag.
config: Use the current media optimization article and the SBC vendor’s build.
fault: Internal users hairpin out to the internet and back to the SBC on the same LAN.

plain: Microsoft’s front end for certain compatible analog and SIP devices that are not Teams phones.
why: It is not a substitute for a certified Direct Routing SBC.
config: Check the current supported device list before you buy handsets.
fault: A generic analog adapter is plugged in and never registers.

plain: A handset in Microsoft’s certified device program, signing in as a Teams user.
why: An uncertified SIP phone will not behave like a Teams client.
config: Buy from the current certified list and assign Teams Phone plus a number.
fault: A bargain SIP phone is forced through SIP Gateway and the feature list is wrong.

plain: The media encryption Direct Routing uses. Signaling is TLS. A successful INVITE with plaintext RTP is not the design.
why: One-way audio is often a port problem, not a missing SRTP checkbox you invent.
config: Allow the UDP media range. Do not strip SRTP on the SBC.
fault: The SBC offers RTP/AVP only and the call fails or is unsupported.

plain: Direct Routing signaling expects modern TLS. TLS 1.0 is not a compatible offer.
why: Old SBC firmware is a certificate problem and a protocol problem at once.
config: Upgrade firmware and offer TLS 1.2 or newer toward the proxies.
fault: The handshake dies before OPTIONS.

plain: The name on the SBC certificate must match the FQDN you paired. Wildcards are allowed when they follow RFC 2818.
why: A certificate that is valid for the website and not for sbc1.contoso.com still fails.
config: Issue the certificate for the paired name. Include the chain.
fault: TLS fails with a name mismatch and someone restarts the SBC.

plain: The SBC certificate must come from a CA in Microsoft’s trusted root program. A private lab CA is not enough for production pairing.
why: Lab trunks that use a private CA teach the wrong lesson.
config: Use a public CA for the production FQDN.
fault: The trunk works in the lab and fails the morning you point it at sip.pstnhub.

plain: The certificate should include the server authentication extended key usage.
why: A client-auth-only certificate is the wrong object.
config: Request the certificate from the SBC’s CSR so the name and the EKU are right.
fault: The chain is trusted and the EKU is still wrong.

plain: The per-user, per-call quality view in the Teams admin center. Use it when one person had one bad call.
why: It will not explain a building. That is CQD.
config: Open the user’s call and read jitter, loss, and RTT on each stream.
fault: A site problem is hunted one user at a time.

plain: The aggregate quality report. Use it for subnets, buildings, and trends.
why: A single angry caller is the wrong entry point.
config: Confirm the subnet-to-building map before you trust a building chart.
fault: HQ looks terrible because the VPN pool was labeled HQ.

plain: Teach yourself to look at jitter, packet loss, and round-trip time separately. A mark of DSCP 0 plus high jitter is a different fault from 12% loss with EF still set.
why: One ‘poor’ label hides the cause.
config: Capture at the egress and compare with CQD.
fault: The ticket says ‘Teams is down’ and loss is 0.2% with a 600 ms RTT.

plain: A time-ordered picture of requests and responses between client, proxy, SBC, and carrier, joined by Call-ID.
why: Without the Call-ID you are looking at two different calls.
config: Capture on the SBC, filter the Call-ID, and read the first non-success code.
fault: Two captures are compared and they are different calls.

plain: Change one thing, then collect the same evidence again. A reboot plus a dial-plan edit plus a firewall change teaches nothing.
why: Voice bridges punish bundled changes.
config: Write the hypothesis, the change, and the capture you expect.
fault: Three vendors change three boxes and the call starts working for an unknown reason.

plain: Microsoft’s contact-center product. It can stand alone or sit with Customer Service. Voice uses Azure Communication Services under the covers.
why: It is not an auto attendant with extra steps.
config: Deploy the environment, the channels, and unified routing before you demo Copilot.
fault: A pilot turns on Copilot and never defines a queue.

plain: The representative experience in Dynamics. Contact Center can embed there or run as its own product surface.
why: Buying Customer Service does not automatically give you the contact-center voice channel.
config: Confirm embedded versus standalone in the current implementation guide.
fault: Agents look for the queue in the wrong app.

plain: The intake pipe in unified routing. It classifies work and sends it to a queue.
why: A channel with no workstream is a number that rings nowhere useful.
config: Create the workstream, then the rules, then the queues.
fault: Chat and voice land in the same queue with no skill rules.

plain: Rules that set skills, intent, or priority on a work item before assignment.
why: Without classification, capacity and skills have nothing to read.
config: Test with two items that should land in different queues.
fault: French callers reach the English queue.

plain: How many items of each type a representative can hold. A voice call usually consumes more than a chat message.
why: Agents look idle in one channel and overloaded in another.
config: Set capacity, then watch a test item get stuck when the number is zero.
fault: The queue has agents and every item overflows.

plain: The human on the contact-center side. AB-250 calls the console the representative experience.
why: Do not confuse this person with a Teams resource account.
config: Give them a security role, a capacity profile, and a queue membership.
fault: The user can open the app and is not a member of any queue.

plain: Assistive summaries, suggested replies, and knowledge inside the representative experience. It is not the PSTN route.
why: A summary of the wrong case is worse than no summary.
config: Connect knowledge sources and test on a known case.
fault: Copilot answers from a stale article and the agent sends it.

plain: The published AB-250 study guide weights channel implementation at about 30–35 percent, the largest slice.
why: People over-study Copilot and under-study voice, chat, and the other channels.
config: Spend the study time on channel setup and routing.
fault: An exam candidate can describe Copilot and cannot trace a voice channel.

plain: A certified contact center attaches to Teams through certified SBCs and Direct Routing.
why: Microsoft’s note: the contact-center agent does not need a phone-system license for that solution; a Teams user who receives a transfer does.
config: Confirm the vendor’s current certification, then design the SBC and the transfer target’s license.
fault: Transfers to experts fail because the expert has no Teams Phone number.

plain: The contact center uses the Teams client, Graph, and Cloud Communications APIs. Teams Phone is the calling system and the agent works in Teams.
why: This is not ‘we also installed their desktop.’
config: Read the Extend section of the contact-center article before you license agents.
fault: The design buys a Connect SBC for an Extend product.

plain: The model Microsoft Learn names, as of 14 October 2026, for a native experience. Partner material describes it as ACS-based applications on Teams calling infrastructure. Older decks say Power. Ask which current model a vendor holds.
why: Licensing and media follow the model, not the sales adjective.
config: Get the vendor’s certification letter and match it to Connect, Extend, or Unify.
fault: A proposal says Power and nobody can find the media path.

plain: A way for a contact center, including Dynamics 365 Contact Center, to use a customer’s existing Teams Phone for the agent’s telephony.
why: It is not a second carrier hidden in the app.
config: Use a solution that has finished the certification if you want the supported experience. The API existing is not the same as a finished certification.
fault: Two phone systems ring the same person.

plain: Cisco Unified Border Element can be the certified SBC between Teams and CUCM or a carrier. The IOS-XE release you run has its own guide.
why: This campus does not paste a production dial-peer.
config: TLS to the three proxies, a certificate whose name matches the paired FQDN, and dial-peers toward CUCM.
fault: Early offer and codec preferences are left at a lab default and calls 488.

plain: During coexistence, either Teams or CUCM should transform numbers, not both.
why: Double +44 is a classic dual-running fault.
config: Write the owner on the design and test a call in each direction.
fault: CUCM adds a prefix and the Teams dial plan adds it again.

plain: A call from a user who stayed on CUCM to a user who moved to Teams hairpins through the SBC. It is normal during dual-running and expensive as a steady state.
why: Media and licenses both feel it.
config: Move groups that call each other in the same wave.
fault: The carrier bill rises and nobody left the building.

plain: A SIP trunk through a local gateway or CUBE can carry calls between Webex Calling users and Teams users during a split estate.
why: Chat interoperability is a different project from voice.
config: Treat it as coexistence with one numbering plan, not as a merger.
fault: Two dial plans both own the same range.

plain: Contact-center agents can stay on CVP and Finesse while knowledge workers move to Teams. The SBC sends contact-center numbers one way and user numbers another.
why: Putting an agent on a Teams client does not keep the CVP script in control.
config: Split the dial plan by number range and test a transfer to an expert on Teams.
fault: Agents move first and the IVR script can no longer see them.

plain: Genesys sells contact-center integrations with Teams. The certification model, Connect, Extend, or Unify, decides the media path and the licenses.
why: Do not assume last year’s diagram.
config: Ask for the current Microsoft certification and design to that model.
fault: The statement of work says certified and does not name the model.

plain: A customer pattern uses an SBC between Teams Direct Routing and Amazon Connect or a SIP voice connector. It is a bridge you design, not a Microsoft Calling Plan feature.
why: Confirm the current vendor docs before you promise agent whisper or recording.
config: Draw the SIP path and the identifier you will store.
fault: Both platforms record and neither capture has the Call-ID.

plain: The ACS server-side calling API. Your app answers, plays, recognizes DTMF or speech, and transfers. You receive events. You do not drive a desktop click.
why: It is the IVR runtime, not the Teams client.
config: Subscribe to the events and time out the recognize step.
fault: The app never answers, so the caller hears ringing until the platform gives up.

plain: The ACS client SDK for a human in a browser or a mobile app. Different from Call Automation, which is the server.
why: Teams interop has its own requirements on top of either one.
config: Pick the SDK if a person is on the page. Pick automation if a bot answers.
fault: A web page uses the calling SDK and nobody handles the server events.

plain: The Call Automation action that collects DTMF or speech. It needs a timeout and a path for ‘none of the above.’
why: A recognize step without an escape traps the caller.
config: Map 0 to a human queue and test it.
fault: The bot repeats the prompt until the caller hangs up.

plain: Microsoft’s speech-to-text and text-to-speech service. Copilot Studio and custom IVRs can use it. It is not emergency calling.
why: A custom neural voice has its own approval rules. Do not assume you can clone a person.
config: Choose a voice you are allowed to use and log the recognition result.
fault: The prompt language does not match the caller and every intent is unknown.

plain: A bot built in Copilot Studio that can front a voice channel, including Dynamics contact-center voice, using topics or generative orchestration.
why: Generative answers still need an escape to a human and a knowledge source you trust.
config: Publish the agent, attach it to the channel, and test the escape digit.
fault: The agent is the only target of the public number, including emergencies.

plain: The Azure portal family for models, agents, and evaluations. The earlier name was Azure AI Studio. It does not route PSTN.
why: A model demo is not a contact-center design.
config: Evaluate a prompt against a test set before you put it on a phone number.
fault: A model change ships to the IVR with no eval.

plain: ACS can be set up to call Teams users and to join Teams meetings when the interop prerequisites are met.
why: A raw ACS number does not automatically become a Teams user.
config: Follow the current interop article for the resource you created.
fault: The bot can call the PSTN and cannot transfer to a Teams expert.

plain: MS-700 is still live, with a skills update on Oct 27 2026; it is NOT retired and has no replacement. It is the exam for Microsoft 365 Certified: Teams Administrator Associate.
why: Rumors that it was replaced by an MS-220 collaboration exam are not what Learn says.
config: Study the current guide, including network and call-quality objectives. There is no replacement exam.
fault: A candidate skips networking because they think the exam is only meetings.

plain: MB-280 retired Jul 31 2026, with AB-210 as its successor; AB-210 is in beta. It covered Sales and Customer Insights, not the contact-center product.
why: People still put it on a contact-center study plan.
config: Do not book MB-280. AB-210 is its successor and is in beta. AB-250 is the contact-center exam.
fault: A job post requires MB-280 after the retirement date.

plain: Dynamics 365 Sales AI Consultant Associate. AB-210 is the successor to MB-280 and is in beta. It is not a replacement for MS-700.
why: It is the wrong exam for a contact-center engineer.
config: Use AB-250 when the job is Dynamics 365 Contact Center. Use AB-210 only for a sales role, and remember it is in beta.
fault: Study time goes to sales Copilot for a queue-routing role.

plain: Transforming Contact Center Experiences with AI in Dynamics 365. It earns Dynamics 365 Contact Center AI Engineer Associate. Pass mark is 700. The public page allows 120 minutes.
why: The beta discount ran through 18 June 2026. Confirm the seat you can book now.
config: Study deploy, channels, agents, work distribution, the representative experience, and analytics.
fault: A candidate revises MB-280 practice tests for this exam.

plain: Azure Fundamentals. It was not on the retirement list reviewed on 14 October 2026.
why: Useful context for ACS and Speech. It will not teach you a dial plan.
config: Take it if you need Azure vocabulary, not instead of MS-700.
fault: A voice design is approved because someone passed AZ-900.

plain: Security, Compliance, and Identity Fundamentals. The English certification is scheduled to update on 21 October 2026.
why: It frames Entra ID and compliance. It does not configure an SBC.
config: Read the current study guide after the 21 October update if you sit it later.
fault: Conditional Access is treated as out of scope for a voice project.

plain: Microsoft 365 Fundamentals retired on 31 March 2026.
why: Do not recommend it as the starting exam.
config: Use role exams and the product docs.
fault: A learning path still tells a new hire to book MS-900.

plain: Azure AI Fundamentals retired on 30 June 2026.
why: Speech and Copilot Studio are learned from their own docs now.
config: Do not use a retired fundamentals exam as the AI plan.
fault: The study plan lists AI-900 beside AB-250.

plain: Microsoft role-based exams, including MS-700 and AB-250, require 700 out of 1000.
why: A practice percentage is not the same scale unless the practice says so.
config: Use the official practice assessment when one exists.
fault: Someone stops studying at a 70 percent practice score on a different scale.

plain: A user starts a recording of a call, meeting, or event. Policy can allow it. The user can stop it. Storage follows meeting rules.
why: It is not a compliance program. Guests cannot start it.
config: Set the meeting, calling, and events policies on purpose.
fault: A regulated desk is told to ‘just hit record.’

plain: A third-party recorder is invited by policy into new calls, meetings, and events. The user does not start it and participant consent is not the control. Notification is enforced.
why: The comparison table says audio-only is not the compliance mode. Media listed is voice, video, and screen share.
config: Create the application instance, enable the policy, grant it, and test a new call.
fault: The policy is granted and nothing records because the bot instance was never created.

plain: The bot instance of a certified recorder. The policy references it. Without it, granting the policy does not record.
why: Work with the recorder vendor for the application ID. Do not invent one.
config: New-CsTeamsComplianceRecordingApplication attaches it to the policy.
fault: Recording works in the vendor’s cloud and never joins the Teams call.

plain: When you grant a compliance recording policy, calls and meetings already up are not swept in. Test with a new call.
why: A pilot that reuses an open meeting proves nothing.
config: Place a fresh call after the grant and confirm the bot joined.
fault: The pilot says recording failed because they watched an old meeting.

plain: Listening to and scoring recorded interactions. Often the same vendor as compliance recording, sometimes a separate one.
why: QM needs the recording first. A score without audio is a rumor.
config: Define the form, the sample, and who may listen.
fault: Supervisors export recordings to a laptop share.

plain: Scheduling and adherence for a queue. It eats interval stats, handle time, and shrinkage. It is not a feature of a Teams user policy.
why: Teams Call Analytics will not staff next Tuesday.
config: Feed offered, answered, abandoned, and handle time from the queue or the CCaaS.
fault: WFM says you were overstaffed while the queue overflowed, because overflow removed the calls from the count.

plain: The fraction of paid time that is not available for contacts: leave, training, meetings, breaks.
why: Erlang C tells you how many people must be on the phone. Shrinkage tells you how many to roster.
config: Publish the assumption. A 30 percent guess should be labeled as a guess.
fault: The schedule staffs the Erlang number and half the team is in training.

plain: Handle time divided by handle time plus available time. High occupancy feels efficient and burns people out.
why: WFM and quality fight here.
config: Watch it beside service level, not instead of service level.
fault: A site celebrates 95 percent occupancy and abandonment climbs.

plain: The fraction of contacts answered inside a target, for example 80 percent in 20 seconds. Erlang C is one teaching model of it.
why: Averages hide the tail.
config: Write the target, the interval, and the abandonment rule.
fault: Two vendors compute abandoned calls differently and both claim the target.

plain: Power BI can sit on top of Call Quality Dashboard data. It does not replace Call Analytics for one call, and it inherits a bad subnet map.
why: A pretty report of the wrong building is still wrong.
config: Fix the building and subnet dimensions before you publish a dashboard.
fault: Leadership sees a red HQ that is actually the VPN pool.

plain: The CRM opens the contact that matches the caller. Teams does not do this by itself for an ordinary PSTN call.
why: The contact center or a middleware has to pass an E.164 number or a case id.
config: Normalize before the lookup. Store the Call-ID on the timeline.
fault: The pop shows the wrong person because the trunk prefix was still on the number.

plain: The international form of a number, starting with + and a country code. Routes and CRM lookups should use it after normalization.
why: Raw digits mean different things in different countries.
config: Normalize first, then route, then look up.
fault: The CRM stores 0207… and the SBC stores +44207… and they never join.

plain: The SIP header that identifies one dialog. It is the join key between an SBC capture, a carrier ticket, and a CRM note.
why: A timestamp is not an identifier. Two calls start in the same second.
config: Write the Call-ID into the system you will have open during an incident.
fault: Support has a CRM case and an SBC log and cannot prove they are the same call.

plain: A named place where another system is allowed to attach: a policy, a queue overflow, a subnet list, an event, an identifier.
why: A seam you do not name becomes a rewrite.
config: Document the seam in the same change as the feature.
fault: Recording is added a year later and the number plan has to change.

plain: A digit or intent that always reaches a person. Voice agents need one. Emergency numbers need a real route, not a bot.
why: A bot that cannot fail open will trap callers.
config: Test the escape on every prompt change.
fault: The prompt says ‘say agent’ and the recognize step has no such intent.

plain: The date the SBC certificate stops being valid. It is an integration hook because every carrier and every proxy will notice it on the same morning.
why: Calendar it like a license, not like a surprise.
config: Monitor the date and renew before the TLS handshake fails.
fault: OPTIONS fail on a Saturday and the dial plan is blamed.

plain: The same subnet definitions should feed emergency location, location-based routing, and the CQD building report.
why: Three spreadsheets drift.
config: Give one team the edit right and publish the list.
fault: E911 says London, CQD says VPN, LBR says Manchester.

plain: A 15-minute or 30-minute bucket of offered, answered, and abandoned contacts. WFM and Erlang C both assume you know the bucket.
why: Mixing daily totals into a 30-minute formula is a unit error.
config: Export the same interval the schedule uses.
fault: The forecast is ten times too high because the interval was a day.

plain: A caller who hangs up before an agent answers. Whether short abandons count is a business rule.
why: Two reports with different abandon rules cannot be compared.
config: Write the rule down and use it in WFM and in the service-level report.
fault: Service level is met only because abandons under five seconds were deleted.

plain: Talk time plus after-call work, unless your definition says otherwise. Erlang traffic is calls times handle time divided by the interval.
why: A handle time that forgets after-call work understaffs the queue.
config: Measure it from the contact center, not from a stopwatch on one call.
fault: The Erlang sheet uses talk time only and the agents never finish wrap-up.

plain: A location object that can be carried in a SIP INVITE for an emergency call so the far end sees where the caller is.
why: It does not replace a carrier who knows how to route emergency calls in that country.
config: Confirm the SBC passes it and the carrier reads it.
fault: The location is stripped at the SBC and the PSAP gets the trunk’s address only.

plain: An emergency calling policy can notify people on site when an emergency call is placed.
why: Security who are not notified will meet the responders in the wrong lobby.
config: Test the notification with the carrier’s test process, not with a real emergency call.
fault: The test notifies nobody because the policy was never assigned.

plain: Office 365 GCC High uses sip.pstnhub.gov.teams.microsoft.us. Do not copy the commercial three-proxy list into a government tenant.
why: The commercial names will not be the signaling peers.
config: Read the plan page for the cloud you are actually in.
fault: A commercial runbook is pasted into GCC High.

plain: Office 365 DoD uses sip.pstnhub.dod.teams.microsoft.us.
why: Same failure as using commercial names in the wrong cloud.
config: Use the DoD name from the current plan page.
fault: The SBC peers with sip.pstnhub.microsoft.com from a DoD tenant.

plain: The plan page also lists sip.ipv6.pstnhub.microsoft.com and the sip2 and sip3 IPv6 names, resolving into 2603:1063:400::/40.
why: An IPv6-only SBC that was given the IPv4 names never peers.
config: Match the address family you actually route.
fault: Firewall objects exist only for IPv4.

plain: Teams Direct Routing presents media in the INVITE. An SBC or CUBE that waits for a delayed offer will negotiate badly.
why: 488 and one-way audio show up when the offer model is wrong.
config: Set the vendor profile for early offer toward Teams.
fault: CUCM sends delayed offer all the way to Teams.

plain: A certified SBC family. Mediant devices and their management tools are common in Direct Routing designs. The Microsoft certified list is the support boundary, the vendor guide is the config.
why: Naming the brand is not a design.
config: Follow AudioCodes’ current Teams document for the firmware you run.
fault: A forum config from 2019 is pasted onto new firmware.

plain: Ribbon’s certified session border controllers are a Direct Routing option. Core and software editions differ.
why: The support path is Ribbon first, then Microsoft if the vendor escalates.
config: Use Ribbon’s current Teams guide and a public certificate.
fault: OPTIONS are answered on the wrong interface.

plain: Oracle Communications Session Border Controller can be certified for Direct Routing on specific releases. Check the Microsoft list for the release, not the logo.
why: An unlisted release is an unsupported trunk.
config: Match the certified software version and the certificate name.
fault: The beautiful config is one release below the certified list.

plain: Cisco Unified Border Element on IOS-XE, when the release is certified, is a normal Direct Routing SBC and the usual bridge to CUCM.
why: CUBE is still an SBC. It does not make Teams ‘speak SCCP.’
config: Use Cisco’s current CUBE for Teams guide. Trust the signaling ranges. Present the paired name.
fault: A voice engineer applies a SIP trunk to CUCM and never peers with the pstnhub names.

plain: Microsoft’s Direct Routing support boundary: you call the SBC vendor, they escalate to Microsoft if they must. Non-certified SBCs can be refused.
why: Opening a Microsoft case with a homemade SBC wastes the outage.
config: Keep the certified-list screenshot with the firmware version.
fault: A ticket is opened with no SBC logs and no firmware.

plain: Fax, door phones, and elevators usually stay on an SBC or SIP Gateway, not on a Teams client.
why: A Calling Plan user license does not give you an elevator phone.
config: Put analog on the SBC design and test the emergency path from that device.
fault: The elevator is moved to Teams as a user and cannot dial during a WAN cut.

plain: A queue can skip agents whose Teams presence says they are busy or in a meeting.
why: An agent who never sets presence will take every serial call or none, depending on the rest of the design.
config: Decide the presence rule and test with one agent in a meeting.
fault: Agents set themselves to Do Not Disturb to leave the queue, and nobody notices for a week.

plain: Agents can be allowed to leave a queue. If you forbid it, staffing math must include breaks or they will dodge in other ways.
why: WFM adherence and the queue opt-out flag are the same argument.
config: Pick one policy and tell the supervisors.
fault: The schedule says five agents and three have opted out.

plain: A queue feature that calls the customer back. The prerequisite article treats callback as a case that needs funding on the resource account.
why: Callback is an outbound PSTN call, not a setting with no carrier.
config: Fund pay-as-you-go or credits, then test one callback.
fault: The option is on and every callback fails.

plain: Microsoft Graph APIs used by Extend and by recording and presence integrations. They are not a SIP trunk.
why: A design that says ‘we will use Graph instead of an SBC’ still needs a PSTN path.
config: Use Graph for the app, and Calling Plans, Operator Connect, or Direct Routing for the telephone network.
fault: Presence is synced and audio is not connected.

plain: The recorder joins as an application because the user’s policy names it. If the bot fails to join, you have a policy, an ID, or a media problem, in that order.
why: Do not start with the carrier.
config: Check Enabled, the application instance, and the grant, then the vendor’s join log.
fault: The carrier is asked for a recording they never made.

plain: Compliance recordings are retained by the partner’s system, not by Teams meeting storage. Convenience recordings follow meeting storage.
why: Legal hold on a mailbox does not automatically hold the partner’s audio.
config: Write the retention in the partner contract and test a restore.
fault: A regulator asks for a call and the partner’s bucket expired.

plain: The QM scorecard. It should cite behaviors you can hear, not vibes.
why: A form that scores ‘professionalism’ without a definition will not survive an argument.
config: Publish the form before you score people.
fault: Agents are coached on a form they have never seen.

plain: Often a QM vendor feature on the agent desktop. Teams compliance recording’s documented media list is voice, video, and screen share inside the Teams session, which is not the same as a silent desktop recorder.
why: Do not claim Teams records the CRM screen unless the product you bought does.
config: If you need the desktop, buy and disclose that recorder.
fault: A privacy review finds a desktop recorder nobody mentioned.

plain: The table that says which subnet is which building in CQD. It is only as good as the subnets you typed.
why: A wrong building makes a dashboard accuse the wrong LAN.
config: Reconcile it with the emergency subnet list.
fault: Facilities rebuilds a floor and both maps stay old.

plain: CQD is an admin report, not a personal call history. The people who can open it are the roles you grant, not every user.
why: A manager with no role will ask for a screenshot instead of access.
config: Grant the smallest role that can see the report.
fault: CQD credentials are shared.

plain: Time the agent spends in the CRM after the caller hangs up. Include it in handle time if your WFM definition says so.
why: Leaving it out makes Erlang C look generous.
config: Define it and measure it from the contact-center state, not from memory.
fault: Agents are ‘available’ in Teams while still writing the case.

plain: Assignment that prefers a representative who has the skill the classification step wrote on the work item.
why: Skills that exist on a slide and not on the user do nothing.
config: Attach skills to people and to the classification rules, then test a miss.
fault: Every item requires a skill nobody has, so the queue never assigns.

plain: Classification that uses an intent, often from a bot or a model, to pick a queue.
why: An intent of ‘unknown’ needs a default queue.
config: Map unknown to a human, not to a retry loop.
fault: The model returns unknown and the caller is played the same prompt.

plain: Contact-center campaigns that place calls outward. They need a number, a consent story, and a capacity plan.
why: They are not a Teams user’s personal redial.
config: Follow the current channel article for outbound, and fund the numbers.
fault: A campaign uses a user’s caller ID and the CRM trust collapses.

plain: A channel feature that can translate a conversation. It is not a substitute for a language queue when the policy says a human must speak the language.
why: Translation errors in a regulated script are your errors.
config: Decide where translation is allowed and where a skilled human is required.
fault: A billing dispute is translated badly and the case notes disagree.

plain: The documents a Copilot or a generative agent is allowed to quote. If the source is wrong, the answer is wrong with confidence.
why: Ground the agent or do not put it on the phone.
config: Limit the sources and test questions whose answers you already know.
fault: The agent quotes a retired price list.

plain: The Copilot Studio mode that chooses topics and tools from the conversation, as opposed to a rigid topic tree.
why: It needs tighter safety because the path is not a single menu.
config: Keep the human escape outside the model’s mood.
fault: The agent talks a caller out of the escape phrase.

plain: The menu-like Copilot Studio design. Predictable and easier to test. Weaker on paraphrase.
why: Use it when the call must follow a script.
config: Write the topics, the entities, and the fallback.
fault: Fallback is empty and the caller hears silence.

plain: One way ACS delivers call events to your app. If the subscription is wrong, your IVR never sees RecognizeCompleted.
why: The call can be up and your code asleep.
config: Log the event type and the call id.
fault: The app polls a database and the events expired.

plain: Digits in the audio path or as telephone-events. IVRs fail when the SBC strips them.
why: A human can talk and the bot never hears 1.
config: Test digits through every SBC, not only Teams-to-Teams.
fault: The queue escape works in the lab and fails through the carrier.

plain: Silence suppression changes the average bitrate. Do not size a link only from a G.711 average that assumed comfort noise you did not enable.
why: The peak is still the number that fills the queue.
config: Size for the codec you offer, per direction, at the packetization you set.
fault: The link was sized for silence and the all-hands call filled it.

plain: The usual voice packet interval in these bandwidth figures. A 10 ms interval doubles the header tax.
why: Changing ptime on the SBC changes the bandwidth you planned.
config: Lock ptime in the design.
fault: One SBC uses 10 ms and the policer drops packets.

plain: The client waits a little so late packets can still be played. Too small and you hear gaps. Too large and you talk over each other.
why: CQD jitter and the buffer are related and not the same number.
config: Fix the network before you hunt a hidden buffer setting.
fault: A WAN with 40 ms jitter is ‘fixed’ by a slide that says buffer.

plain: How long a packet takes to go and come back. Long RTT with low loss means distance or hairpin, not a dirty cable.
why: People add bandwidth and the delay stays.
config: Look at the path. Bypass or local egress may beat a fatter pipe.
fault: A branch backhauls media across a continent.

plain: A router or VPN that sets the mark back to 0. The client did its job and the path undid it.
why: Verify at the egress, not only on the PC.
config: Capture outside the VPN.
fault: The laptop shows EF and the WAN sees 0.

plain: People who join meetings in a browser do not use the fixed 50000-range client ports. An ACL that only matches those ports misses them.
why: QoS designs that ignore browsers miss a real population.
config: Say so in the design if many people join from browsers.
fault: Guests sound worse and the ACL is declared complete.

plain: Mac, iOS, and Android use hard-coded audio EF and a hard-coded video and sharing mark. They are not the Windows policy object.
why: A Windows-only QoS rollout looks done and is not.
config: Still enable QoS in the admin center, and mark at the network for devices that will not cooperate.
fault: Mobile executives are the poor-quality population.

plain: The current Teams client process name used when you bind a Windows QoS policy. An old policy aimed at the classic client marks nothing.
why: Policy that matches the wrong executable is a silent miss.
config: Update the policy object and verify with a capture.
fault: QoS policy still names the previous client.

plain: The hour you actually size. Average day divided by eight is not a busy hour.
why: Erlang inputs are busy-interval numbers.
config: Take the busy interval from the contact center, not from a yearly average.
fault: The link is fine at 11:00 and dead at 09:15.

plain: Both PBX and Teams carry live numbers during a move. Rollback needs the old route left intact.
why: A cut with no rollback is a career event.
config: Move a range, keep the old path, and write the backout.
fault: The old trunk is deleted on Friday.

plain: Moving a public number from one carrier to another. It has a date and a letter of authority. It is not a PowerShell metaphor.
why: Direct Routing can use numbers the carrier already holds, so a port might be unnecessary.
config: Confirm who owns the number before you promise a weekend cut.
fault: Two carriers route the same number on Monday.

plain: What outbound calls present. Resource-account outbound and user outbound are different policies.
why: A queue that presents a user’s mobile number breaks trust.
config: Set the calling identity on the voice app on purpose.
fault: Customers return a call and reach an employee’s personal desk.

plain: The audio a queue plays while a caller waits. Licensing and the file both matter, and silence is a choice you should make on purpose.
why: Callers who hear nothing hang up, and abandon looks like a staffing crisis.
config: Upload a file you have rights to, and test the timeout.
fault: A licensed song is uploaded.

plain: A respectable overflow target when nobody is left to answer. It depends on Cloud Voicemail and a mailbox for the account that owns it.
why: Overflow to voicemail without a mailbox is a dead end.
config: Test the overflow, then check that the message arrived.
fault: Callers are offered voicemail and the message is never deposited.

plain: The public number on the first voice app. Everything else can be an internal target.
why: People buy a number per menu option and then cannot afford to change the menu.
config: One number, many targets, overflow included.
fault: Each menu option is a ported number and the carrier lead time runs the project.

plain: Compliance recording and many Teams policies can be assigned to a group. A user in the wrong group is recorded, or not, as a consequence.
why: Group sprawl is a voice defect.
config: Use a group you can explain, and read the effective policy.
fault: A contractor group inherits recording and a privacy review fails.

plain: The policy the user actually has after direct assignment and group assignment are resolved. The one you edited may not be it.
why: Get-CsOnlineUser beats the portal memory.
config: Read the effective value before and after the change.
fault: You update a policy that is not assigned.

plain: A tenant that is not production. Pair a lab SBC there. Do not discover certificate behavior on the company trunk.
why: Production is where rollback costs money.
config: Keep lab domains and lab certificates obvious.
fault: A lab FQDN is the production FQDN.

plain: Cmdlet parameters move between MicrosoftTeams module versions. Read help in the version you are about to run.
why: A blog’s parameter list is not a contract.
config: Get-Help cmdlet -Parameter * in the lab.
fault: A script from last year removes a number.

plain: Use the telephony or communications role that can do the task. Global Administrator is not a voice habit.
why: A shared global account makes every later audit useless.
config: Named admin accounts, voice roles, and Conditional Access for admins.
fault: The SBC password and the global admin password are the same sticky note.

plain: A number assigned to a resource account or conferencing, as opposed to a user’s personal number. The inventory and the license follow the connectivity option.
why: A user number on a queue is how you lose the queue when the human leaves.
config: Take service numbers from the carrier or Calling Plan inventory you actually have.
fault: The receptionist leaves and the main number leaves with them.

plain: What Teams does with a number you own that is not assigned. Routing it to an attendant is a product choice you should make.
why: Silence on a published-but-unassigned number looks like an outage.
config: Point unknown numbers at an attendant or a message.
fault: A ported block has fifty silent numbers.

plain: This campus treats repeated missed OPTIONS as a reason to pull a trunk. It does not publish Microsoft’s internal counter as if it were a documented integer.
why: A lab timer is not a contractual timer.
config: Watch the admin-center SBC status and the SBC’s own OPTIONS log together.
fault: Someone sets a script to fail over after one missed packet and flaps the trunk.

plain: Pull the primary proxy or the primary SBC in a window and prove the next one takes calls.
why: A second gateway that has never received a call is a drawing.
config: Rehearse, then put the result in the runbook.
fault: The outage is the first test.

plain: If the SBC and Teams offer no codec in common, the call fails, often with 488.
why: Adding AMR-WB on a bypass trunk does not fix a G.711 refusal.
config: Offer G.711 at minimum unless you have a measured reason not to.
fault: The SBC allows only G.729 and the far end does not.

plain: A-law and μ-law are both G.711. A trunk that offers the wrong one still often interoperates, and sometimes does not. Offer both if the carrier is vague.
why: This is a one-line SBC change, after you have a capture.
config: Capture SDP and compare.
fault: A new country is added and audio sounds like noise.

plain: The words the queue plays about position or wait. A lie (‘your call is important’) is still a design choice you can decline.
why: Bad messages increase abandon.
config: Say something true: whether you record, and whether you call back.
fault: The message promises a callback the queue cannot place.

plain: Both convenience and compliance recording require participant notification. Compliance does not ask the participant for consent in the comparison Microsoft publishes.
why: A silent compliance recorder is a legal problem, not a clever config.
config: Confirm the partner’s announcement and test it.
fault: Notification is off because it ‘hurt the experience.’

plain: Know whether your recorder and your policy include emergency calls, and follow the rule you were given. Do not route emergency calls into a bot so they can be ‘handled.’
why: Emergency is a route, a location, and a carrier.
config: Keep the emergency voice route boring and local.
fault: 999 matches the IVR workstream.

plain: The case note should carry the Call-ID, the number in E.164, the queue, and the agent. Then a later complaint can be found.
why: A note that says ‘called customer’ cannot be audited.
config: Make the screen pop write those fields.
fault: The case exists and the recording cannot be found.

plain: A seam left on purpose for a system you might add later, using a product that already exists. It is not a promise that Microsoft will ship a feature.
why: Invented roadmap items fail audits.
config: Name the hook, the identifier, and the failure if you skip it.
fault: A design depends on an unannounced SBC feature.

plain: Older conversation says Power for the third contact-center model. The Learn article maintained on 14 October 2026 says Unify, Extend, and Connect.
why: Using the old word without a mapping hides the media path.
config: Ask the vendor which of the three current models they hold.
fault: The contract says Power and the network team opens no ports.

plain: The list of SBCs and contact-center solutions changes. A campus page is not the list.
why: Quote the list the week you buy.
config: Link the design to the current Microsoft page and the firmware.
fault: A purchase order cites a 2022 PDF.

plain: In the Connect model, Microsoft’s documentation says the contact-center side does not need a phone-system license, and the Teams user who receives a transferred call does need Teams Phone and a number.
why: Experts who ‘just answer in Teams’ still need a telephone.
config: License the humans who receive transfers.
fault: The agent transfers and the expert’s client will not take the PSTN call.

plain: A Dynamics or Teams trial proves a click path. It does not prove emergency calling, recording retention, or a busy hour.
why: Pilots skip the boring gates.
config: Write the gates: 911, recording, overflow, certificate, rollback.
fault: The pilot is declared production on Friday.

plain: The numbers go back to the old route if the new path fails. If you deleted the old route, you do not have a rollback.
why: Dual-running exists so rollback is a script, not a rebuild.
config: Keep the old trunk until the new path has a quiet week.
fault: The maintenance window ends with no public numbers.

plain: Call-ID, the policy you read, the ladder, and the CQD or Call Analytics row. One pack per hypothesis.
why: Verbal ‘it failed’ is not a pack.
config: Store the pack with the change ticket.
fault: The same outage is debugged from scratch next month.

plain: A fictional tenant name used in Microsoft samples and in this campus. It is not a customer.
why: Examples use 555 numbers and example domains so nothing here is someone’s directory.
config: Keep lab names obviously fake.
fault: A lab script is aimed at a real tenant by find-and-replace.

plain: Microsoft’s practice UI for what an exam looks like. It is not the product lab.
why: Use it so the tool is not a surprise. Still study the skills.
config: Open the sandbox once before the appointment.
fault: The first time someone sees a lab item is during the exam.

plain: Role-based certifications expire unless you pass the free renewal on Learn. Retirement is a different event from expiry.
why: A certification you earned and did not renew is not a retirement of the exam.
config: Calendar the renewal. Re-read what changed.
fault: MS-700 lapses and the holder thinks the exam was retired.

plain: When this campus and a study guide disagree, the study guide accessed the week you sit the exam wins.
why: Skills move. The 27 October 2026 MS-700 update is an example.
config: Re-open the guide before you book.
fault: A candidate memorizes a third-party brain dump.

plain: The device that speaks SIP to Teams and SIP or another protocol to the carrier or PBX, and enforces the edge.
why: Without a certified one, Direct Routing is unsupported.
config: Pair the FQDN, not a nickname.
fault: A router with SIP ALG is described as the SBC.

plain: A firewall feature that rewrites SIP. It breaks Direct Routing more often than it helps.
why: Microsoft’s network guidance does not want helpers in the media path.
config: Turn SIP ALG off on the path to the proxies.
fault: INVITEs are rewritten and the contact header points at a private address.

plain: Teams must be able to reach the SBC. A purely private address with no public path will not pair.
why: NAT without a stable signaling address is a classic failure.
config: Publish the signaling address you documented.
fault: The SBC is only reachable on a VPN Microsoft is not on.

plain: Proxy addresses change inside the published ranges. A firewall object built from one lookup goes stale.
why: Allow the range, not the A record you saw today.
config: Re-read the plan page when you edit the firewall.
fault: The trunk fails after a resolver change and the certificate is blamed.

plain: The plan page says that if you enable mutual TLS, install the Microsoft trusted roots on the SBC.
why: MTLS is optional in many designs and mandatory in the way you configured.
config: Match the SBC setting to what you intended.
fault: The SBC demands a client certificate Teams is not presenting in the mode you chose.

plain: The gateway setting that allows media to skip Microsoft’s processors. It is not implied by a short ping.
why: Leave it off until the path is drawn.
config: Set it on the paired gateway, then test from the real subnet.
fault: It is enabled tenant-wide in someone’s notes and only one site can route to the SBC.

plain: The default media path through Microsoft media processors in the region closest to the call.
why: Use it when bypass is unsafe.
config: Allow the documented UDP ranges.
fault: Bypass is off and those ranges are still closed, so audio never starts.

plain: Media processors exist in multiple regions. Calls prefer a close one. You do not pick a street address for the processor.
why: A hairpin to a distant egress undoes that preference.
config: Keep egress local.
fault: European users egress in another continent and RTT follows.

plain: A user can be licensed and still not be enabled for Enterprise Voice in the way the tenant expects. Read the user before you test.
why: The symptom is a client that never offers a dial pad.
config: Read the voice attributes and the license together.
fault: The dial pad is missing and the SBC is rebooted.

plain: A Teams calling policy controls client calling features. It is not the voice routing policy that selects an SBC.
why: Two policies with similar names get granted backwards.
config: Grant the routing policy and the calling policy on purpose.
fault: Outbound PSTN is blocked by a calling policy and the route is blamed.

plain: Presenting a service number instead of a personal mobile. It is a policy, not a hope.
why: Wrong caller ID breaks return calls and CRM trust.
config: Set it on the user or the resource account you mean.
fault: Customers call back a personal mobile that was never the company number.

plain: Teams translations use tokens such as $1 for a capture group. The first matching rule applies the translation and stops.
why: A $1 with no group copies nothing useful.
config: Test the rule with the raw digit string.
fault: The translation says +1$1 and the pattern never captured a group.

plain: A short rule can turn a 4-digit extension into E.164. It must not run before emergency codes.
why: Extensions and short codes share a length problem.
config: Order the rules and test 112, 999, 911, and an extension.
fault: 112 becomes an extension and leaves via the wrong trunk.

plain: The attendant’s holiday set replaces business hours for those dates.
why: Next year’s holidays are a December project.
config: Load them when you build the attendant.
fault: The office is closed and the queue still rings.

plain: The attendant’s operator is where zero, and many failures, should land.
why: An attendant with no operator drops people who do not match a menu.
config: Name a person or a queue.
fault: Callers who press nothing are disconnected.

plain: Directory search should list only the people you intend callers to reach.
why: A wide directory publishes privileged accounts.
config: Scope it.
fault: A caller reaches an executive because search was unrestricted.

plain: Serial routing uses the order of the agent list. Round robin does not.
why: The person on top of a serial list takes the punishment.
config: Pick the method that matches the promise to the team.
fault: One agent receives every call and the others look idle.

plain: How long the caller waits before overflow. Too short and overflow is the product. Too long and they abandon.
why: Test with agents busy.
config: Set it in the queue and call it.
fault: Timeout is a few seconds and nobody is ever answered.

plain: The audio file must be one you have the right to play. A popular song is not a free hold track.
why: Licensing the song is a legal problem, not a Teams setting.
config: Use a file you own or have licensed.
fault: A commercial track is uploaded as hold music.

plain: Where calls go when the attendant is closed. Voicemail, another number, or a message.
why: Closed with no target is a hang-up.
config: Set it and call after hours, or fake the schedule in a lab.
fault: Night calls ring the daytime queue.

plain: A named place in the Teams network topology. Subnets attach to it. Emergency addresses and LBR attach to that story.
why: A site with no subnets does nothing.
config: Create the site, then the subnets, then the address.
fault: The address exists and no subnet points at it.

plain: Civic addresses are validated. An unvalidated string is not a location you can trust.
why: A typo in the street number sends responders next door.
config: Validate, then test from a known subnet.
fault: The address was typed and never validated.

plain: Wi-Fi clients can roam across subnets that do not match the building you think. The subnet you mapped is the location you will send.
why: A café SSID bridged to HQ is a false floor.
config: Map only networks you control.
fault: Guest Wi-Fi is inside the HQ subnet.

plain: Clients must be able to use the appliance when the cloud path is gone. An appliance with no client configuration is a spare server.
why: Read the current SBA article for how clients select it.
config: Test with the WAN blocked, from a phone on that site.
fault: The appliance is powered on and no client knows it.

plain: The SBA still needs a PSTN path. That is the local SBC and carrier, not a cloud media processor you cannot reach.
why: Survival without a local trunk is a slogan.
config: Prove a PSTN call with the WAN down.
fault: The WAN test blocks Microsoft 365 and the only carrier path was through that same WAN.

plain: Rooms need the same DSCP plan as PCs, using the rooms guidance for Windows and Android.
why: A room that sounds worse than a laptop is often unmarked.
config: Include the room subnet in the ACL.
fault: Only user PCs were marked.

plain: The phone signs in as its own account. Voicemail and caller ID follow that account.
why: A shared PIN on a former employee’s account is a privacy incident.
config: Create the device account and the number.
fault: The hallway phone opens a person’s mailbox.

plain: A policy that requires a compliant interactive PC will block a phone or a room.
why: The failure looks like a bad password.
config: Scope a device path you can explain.
fault: Rooms fail on Monday after a security baseline.

plain: Certification is specific about software. ‘We own AudioCodes’ is not a version.
why: Upgrade without checking the list can move you off support.
config: Record the version next to the list date.
fault: The SBC was upgraded on Friday off the certified train.

plain: Both sides must agree the media is SRTP. A gateway forced to RTP/AVP will not complete a normal Direct Routing call.
why: Silence or a failed offer follows.
config: Capture SDP and read the profile.
fault: The carrier leg is SRTP and the Teams leg was stripped.

plain: The SDP way digits are carried so an IVR can see them even when the audio codec would hide tones.
why: In-band tones through a lossy codec disappear.
config: Offer telephone-event and test a digit.
fault: The bot never hears 1 and the talk path is fine.

plain: The header that stays with a SIP dialog so two logs can be proved to be one call.
why: Timestamps collide.
config: Copy it into the ticket and the CRM.
fault: Two engineers compare two different INVITEs.

plain: Who the request claims to be, and who it is for. A normalization bug shows up here as a duplicated country code.
why: Read them before you read codecs.
config: Compare them to the dialed E.164.
fault: The To header contains +4444… and the carrier rejects it.

plain: The media description inside the INVITE when early offer is used. Codecs, ports, and SRTP live here.
why: A 488 is an SDP argument.
config: Read the offer and the answer.
fault: The offer lists a codec the other side rejected.

plain: A commonly taught CQD clue is to treat sustained jitter around 30 ms as painful. Confirm the current data dictionary before you quote a threshold as policy.
why: The clue is a starting point, not a statute.
config: Pair the number with DSCP and the path.
fault: A ticket cites a threshold and nobody captured the packets.

plain: Packet loss near 10 percent is a widely used teaching line for a poor stream. Verify the current CQD definition before you automate an alert on it.
why: Loss and jitter are different faults.
config: Look at loss separately from RTT.
fault: Bandwidth is added for a path whose loss is near zero and whose RTT is 600 ms.

plain: CQD’s subnet field is only useful if you built the building map from real subnets.
why: A typo relocates a building.
config: Reconcile with the emergency list.
fault: 10.8.0.0/16 is named Headquarters.

plain: The unit unified routing assigns: a call, a chat, a case. It is not a Teams message.
why: Capacity is counted in work items.
config: Watch one test item cross classification.
fault: Items vanish because no queue will accept them.

plain: Representatives receive work only from queues they belong to.
why: A license without membership is a spectator.
config: Add the person to the queue and set capacity above zero.
fault: The queue has users and still overflows.

plain: The Dataverse role that lets a representative open the app and touch the rows they should.
why: Teams admin is not this role.
config: Assign the contact-center role the current guide names.
fault: The user sees a blank console.

plain: Contact Center can sit inside Customer Service or stand as its own app. Agents must be told which one they open.
why: The pilot URL is not tribal knowledge.
config: Write the URL and the mode in the design.
fault: Agents look in the wrong app and report an outage.

plain: The classification result you get when the model or the rules do not know. It needs a queue.
why: A loop is not a bucket.
config: Route unknown to humans.
fault: Unknown replays the same prompt.

plain: A draft of the conversation for the representative. It can be wrong. The representative still owns what is sent.
why: A wrong summary in the case file becomes the record.
config: Test on a known case.
fault: The summary names the wrong product and is saved.

plain: The date on the source the bot is allowed to quote. Retired prices stay retired only if you remove them.
why: Grounding in a stale library is confident nonsense.
config: Review sources on a schedule.
fault: The bot quotes last year’s fee.

plain: The classic-topic path when nothing else matches. Empty fallback is silence.
why: Write a sentence and an escape.
config: Test an utterance you did not train.
fault: The caller hears nothing after a novel sentence.

plain: The usual human escape. It has to be implemented, not merely printed on a slide.
why: Test it after every prompt edit.
config: Press 0 in the lab and in production pilot.
fault: The prompt mentions zero and the recognize step ignores it.

plain: The Teams user who receives a PSTN transfer needs Teams Phone and a number in the Connect model’s description.
why: Chat-only experts cannot take the call.
config: License the humans on the transfer list.
fault: Finance is chat-only and every transfer fails.

plain: Some Connect providers share SBC infrastructure across customers. Your routing must still isolate your numbers.
why: A shared SBC is not a shared dial plan.
config: Confirm the provider’s isolation story.
fault: A test number lands in another customer’s tenant.

plain: The carrier document that allows a number to move. Porting without it does not happen.
why: A weekend cut that assumes the port is done will strand the number.
config: Confirm the port date in writing.
fault: Both carriers route the number on Monday.

plain: The old path left in place so numbers can return. Deleting it is not a cleanup. It is the removal of the safety.
why: Keep it until the new path has a quiet week.
config: Write the backout steps.
fault: The maintenance window ends with no public route.

plain: Many Teams policies, including compliance recording, can target a group. Membership changes the effective policy without a click on the user.
why: A contractor group can inherit recording.
config: Read the effective policy after group changes.
fault: Recording starts for people who were only added to a mail group.
